steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Memory is the process of encoding, storing and retrieving information. Encoding converts sensory input into a storable form; storage retains it; retrieval accesses it when needed.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The Multi-Store Model (Atkinson & Shiffrin, 1968): Sensory memory (brief, capacity limited by senses) -> Short-term memory (limited capacity 7+/-2 items, duration ~30 seconds) -> Long-term memory (potentially unlimited capacity and duration) via rehearsal.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Types of LTM: Episodic (personal experiences, e.g. your first day at school), Semantic (facts and knowledge, e.g. Paris is the capital of France), Procedural (skills and actions, e.g. riding a bike).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Eyewitness testimony is unreliable: Loftus & Palmer (1974) showed leading questions distort recall - participants estimated faster speeds when verbs like 'smashed' were used. Anxiety, weapon focus and post-event discussion also reduce accuracy.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Describe the multi-store model of memory and evaluate its strengths and limitations. | Explain how leading questions can affect the accuracy of eyewitness testimony, referring to Loftus & Palmer's research. | Compare and contrast episodic, semantic and procedural long-term memory.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: STM has a capacity of 7+/-2 items and a duration of about 30 seconds. Eyewitness testimony is unreliable - always mention Loftus & Palmer when discussing EWT. Episodic = events you experienced. Semantic = facts you know. Procedural = things you can do.
